understanding.does: You sell a post-quantum cryptographic verification layer to institutions and developers who need to verify transactions before settlement, without changing existing infrastructure.
understanding.standsOut: You are betting on being the first dedicated post-quantum verification layer that works on top of existing settlement rails.

constraint.text: No institution or developer has used QuFi and got a result yet.

evidence: Performance figures (10,000+ nodes, 100,000+ verifications per second) are stated as targets, not measured results.
200+ organisations described as 'in pipeline', not as signed or live customers.
No product has a price, a trial, or a completed deployment shown in any source.
The conclusion page lists 'next steps' including 'expand network participation' and 'deploy enterprise solutions', confirming the network is not yet deployed at scale.

tensions: You sell a running verification network. Nothing on your site or in any page shows it running: no live node, no completed verification, no integration output, no result from any of the three products. | This means every performance number (10,000+ nodes, 100,000+ verifications per second, 2-second finality) is a target on paper, and a buyer has to decide whether to engage before seeing the system do anything.

You claim 200+ organisations in your pipeline across 50+ countries. Not one of them is named, quoted, or described anywhere on your site. | This means an institution evaluating QuFi cannot see who else has looked at it or why they stayed, so every conversation starts from scratch with no peer reference to lean on.

You present three named products. Your site shows no price, no way to buy, no trial, and no contact path for any of them. | This means a buyer who finishes reading your technical case has nowhere to go, so the site functions as a whitepaper distribution point rather than a commercial entry point.

You are speaking to regulated banks, blockchain developers, and individual node operators at the same time. Every page uses the same voice and depth for all three. | This means none of the three audiences gets a path that speaks to their specific decision, so the site reads as a protocol document rather than a sales conversation with any one buyer.
unanswered: Which of the three products (QuVault, QuSettle, QuFi Verify) is the one you are actually trying to sell first, and to which specific buyer type?
What does a real engagement with one of the 200+ pipeline organisations look like right now: a signed agreement, a pilot, a letter of intent, or an email conversation?
What is the intended path from the whitepaper or API documentation to a paying customer?

correction replies: QuFi has no production network running yet, no signed customers, and the 200+ organisations are conversations and expressed interest, not contracts or commitments. The team is technical and you have not yet decided which enterprise buyer you are going after first. / The tension I flagged about claiming a 'running verification network' with nothing to show is now sharper: the site presents QuFi as an operating product when you are still pre-launch, which is a bigger gap than a credibility problem. It is a positioning problem. The 200+ pipeline figure also reads differently now: it is a signal of market curiosity, not validated demand, so leaning on it publicly before you have a named first buyer works against you. / The three-audience problem still stands exactly as it was. You are speaking to regulated banks, blockchain developers, and node operators in the same voice on the same pages, and you have not yet picked your first enterprise buyer. That decision will force the focus the site currently lacks.

You are saying that for a pre-launch protocol, the first buyer is not a revenue event, it is a proof event. You need one institution, even a smaller one with less commercial upside, that runs QuFi in production so you can say 'we did it here' and let that story carry the next ten conversations. / This changes how I read the pipeline tension. I had flagged 200+ unnamed organisations as a credibility gap, implying you needed to name bigger names or close bigger terms. You are telling me the priority is the opposite: get one real production deployment on the board, whatever the size, because that reference is what turns the other 200 from a list into a funnel. / The site still shows no live verification, no integration output, and no completed run of any product, which means even the one reference buyer you land will have nothing to point their peers to when they visit QuFi to check the story for themselves.

You have a mid-tier European bank already in conversation with you, and they have told you exactly what they need to move forward: a security audit of the protocol, a testnet they can run on their own, and one named engineer they can call directly. You are treating this relationship as the reference story worth more than three faster but thinner integrations. / I had flagged that not one of your 200+ pipeline organisations is named or described anywhere, and I read that as a uniform gap across the whole pipeline. This correction tells me at least one relationship is real, specific, and close enough that the bank has given you a concrete list of requirements. The work now is not to prove the pipeline exists; it is to clear those three specific gates for this one bank and let that story do the selling to the next ten. / The tension around a named, dedicated engineer still connects directly to what I said about your site speaking to everyone at once with no page written for any one audience. A regulated bank that needs a single human they can call is exactly the kind of buyer who will not self-serve through a generic product page, so that gap in how you present QuFi still needs closing even as you move this deal forward.

The testnet is in development but not ready for external use, and that is the single thing that has to move before anything else can. The audit runs in parallel and the engineer is just whoever you assigned to it, so neither of those is holding you up. The testnet being live for external use is the 60-day target that everything else waits on. / I had read the audit and the testnet as roughly equal blockers sitting in sequence. That was wrong. The audit is a parallel track you can schedule now, and the testnet is the only gate that matters. This also sharpens tension one from the current understanding: the site showing nothing running is not just a credibility gap, it is a direct reflection of a real technical state. The network is not yet ready for anyone outside your team to touch. / The pipeline of 200-plus organisations across 50-plus countries still sits unverified and unnamed on your site, and that tension does not move until the testnet is live and you have something real to show those organisations.

The mid-tier European bank is not a cold lead or a number in a count. Your security team has already sat with theirs, the relationship is warm, and a second EU bank inside the same regulatory circle is lined up behind them. The testnet is the specific gate both banks are waiting on before they move. / I had folded this bank into the undifferentiated '200+ organisations' claim and treated the whole pipeline as unverifiable. That was wrong. You have at least two named, sequenced, relationship-stage prospects where the blocker is a concrete technical milestone, not a sales conversation. The tension I flagged about no named or described pipeline entry still applies to the site, but it does not apply to the actual pipeline. / The testnet being the gate confirms what I said about your site showing nothing running. Until the testnet is live and visible, even a warm bank relationship has nothing to point at, so closing that gap is still the most urgent thing you need to do.

The next 60 days have one job: get the testnet to a state where a real bank's security team can run their own tests against it. Not a demo, not a walkthrough, a live environment they can probe themselves. / This corrects how I read the 'nothing running' tension. The gap is not that you have no proof of life at all. It is that the testnet is not yet hardened enough to hand to a hostile, credentialed security team. That is a specific engineering milestone, not a general credibility problem, and the 60-day clock is already running against it. / The pipeline of 200+ organisations still has no named institution behind it, and the first bank's security team running against your testnet is the moment that changes. Until one bank signs off, that number stays unverifiable to anyone outside your conversations.
conversation:
BB: I have read what you gave me on QuFi Network. One thing stands out before we talk: you are 60 days from a testnet that a real bank's security team will run against, and your site reads like a published thesis, not a sales motion.
You claim 200+ pipeline organisations across 50+ countries, but no named partner, quote, or case anywhere on the site.
Three products are described with equal weight, so a regulated bank landing on the site cannot tell which one is the door they should walk through first.
The testnet deadline makes the next 60 days a forcing function: what the site says and what you can actually demo need to match before that security review happens.
Which of the three products is the one you are actually trying to close first, and with which specific buyer type.
Which product are you leading with, and for whom?

FOUNDER: The bank's security team will run an end-to-end verification of a real 
transaction flow: they submit a transaction, our node verifies it, and 
they receive a signed proof they can validate independently. If they 
can reproduce that on their own infrastructure without our engineers 
on the call, we've passed.

BB: That is a sharp definition of 'passed': self-sufficient reproduction, no hand-holding. Which means the test is not really about cryptography, it is about documentation and developer experience. The bank's security team needs to run it cold, so whatever they read before they touch the node has to be complete enough to get them there alone. That is a different problem from building the testnet itself.

Which product does this transaction flow belong to: QuSettle, QuVault, or something that sits underneath all three, and is this bank the first institution you are running it with?

FOUNDER: API references exist. QPL onboarding is partial — a developer can read 
it but needs our team for the first setup. Environment setup is 
manual today. All three would need to be tightened before a bank's 
team can run solo. That's the real work of the next 60 days.

BB: So the 60-day goal is actually a documentation and developer-experience sprint, not a cryptography problem. The node works; the gap is that a cold security team cannot yet get from zero to a validated proof without your engineers on the call. That is a solvable problem, but it is a different one from what the site implies.

Which of the three products does this bank's transaction flow actually run through: QuSettle, QuVault, or a core verification layer that sits underneath all three?

FOUNDER: Both. Two of the warm contacts are actively waiting for the testnet 
date — they've asked us twice. The rest are warm introductions that 
went quiet. The 60-day clock is real for the two active ones; for the 
rest, we need the testnet live before they re-engage.

mirror.founderWords: Two warm contacts are actively waiting for the testnet date and have asked twice.
mirror.against: QPL onboarding is partial: a developer can read it but needs our team for the first setup. Environment setup is manual today. All three would need to be tightened before a bank's team can run solo.
mirror.tension: You're telling two banks the testnet is coming, but the thing they need to run it solo isn't ready yet.

strategy.bet: Make the testnet self-serviceable for the two warm contacts who are already waiting
strategy.over: Reaching new pipeline contacts or building broader awareness before the first bank can run solo
tradeOffs: The quiet pipeline said they are waiting for the testnet to be live. Contacting them before it is self-serviceable just burns the relationship again.
The goal is a bank that can reproduce the flow without you. A demo you control proves nothing to a security team. Letting them run it themselves is the actual test.
The two contacts who matter are not reading your site to decide. They are waiting for a testnet date. Site work right now is effort spent on the wrong problem.
notNow: Leave the quiet pipeline alone for now. They told you they are waiting for the testnet. Reaching out before it is ready just reminds them it is still not done.
Set the site aside for this sprint. The bank's security team is not deciding based on your homepage. Fix the product gap first, then fix the story.
Do not open up developer or node operator acquisition right now. You have one job: get one bank's security team through the full flow on their own. Everything else waits.
reconsider: If either warm contact runs the testnet solo and the flow breaks or the proof cannot be independently validated, the bet shifts from product readiness to a deeper technical problem that needs scoping before any marketing move.

If QPL onboarding or environment setup cannot be made self-serviceable within 30 days, the 60-day window closes and you need to decide whether to run a guided evaluation with your engineers present as a fallback.
If one warm contact passes the solo run and publicly confirms it, the quiet pipeline re-engages on its own and the next bet becomes how to handle multiple simultaneous evaluations.

week.context: Week 1 of your 60-day push to make the testnet self-serviceable for the two warm contacts who are already waiting.
week.statement: This week you find every place your team is the product.
week.whyNow: The two warm contacts are ready to test, but the current setup requires your engineers for first onboarding and manual environment configuration.

chapters.title: Write down every step your team carries
chapters.why: You cannot remove yourself from a step you have not named yet.

chapters.title: Replace each intervention with one artifact
chapters.why: A scripted command or config file does the same job your engineer does, without the call.

chapters.title: Assemble the artifacts into one guide
chapters.why: A bank security engineer needs one document to hand around, not a folder of loose files.

today.move: Walk the QPL onboarding flow and write down every step your team touches.
today.detail: Go through first setup as if you are the bank engineer. Every time you reach for a teammate, a manual command, or a config you hold in your head, write it down: what the step is, what is missing, and what form the fix needs to take.

week.doneLooksLike: A written list naming each intervention point, what the bank engineer would need to do instead, and what is currently missing to make that step self-contained.

email.subject: Testnet date and self-service setup guide
email.body:
Hi [Name],

Thank you for your patience. We know you have asked twice and we want to give you a real answer, not another placeholder.

We are targeting [testnet start date] for your team to run the QuFi testnet on your own infrastructure. We will confirm that date by [confirmation date].

When we confirm, you will get one link: a self-service setup guide your engineers can follow start to finish. No demo, no sales call, no changes to your existing environment. Your team runs it, submits a real transaction, receives a signed proof, and validates the result independently. You own the output.

Before we send that guide, we are working through every step where a bank engineer might hit a wall, QPL onboarding, environment configuration, anything that currently needs us in the room. We want to make sure you can go from zero to a validated proof without waiting on us.

One ask: can you tell us your preferred start window around [testnet start date]? That lets us hold the slot and get the guide to you before you begin.

Reply here or book directly at [scheduling link].

Thanks,
[Your name]
QuFi Network
